objectives: Explain how residuals keep gradients flowing
Describe the residual stream as a shared bus

slides.title: Part 1 — Why depth used to be impossible
slides.body: Before residual connections, *adding layers made networks train worse* — not overfit, train worse. One line of algebra removed the ceiling on depth and made modern deep learning possible.

slides.title: The vanishing / exploding gradient wall
slides.body:
Backprop through an $L$-layer plain stack multiplies $L$ per-layer Jacobians. Let each have spectral norm $\approx r$. The gradient reaching layer 1 scales like $r^{L}$. If $r<1$ (the typical case with squashing nonlinearities) then $r^{L}\to 0$ exponentially — early layers receive ~no learning signal (**vanishing**). If $r>1$, $r^{L}\to\infty$ (**exploding**). Either way the usable depth is capped: a 48-layer plain transformer's loss barely moves with the same data/LR a residual one trains fine on. This wasn't a tuning problem — it was structural.

> **Context:** He et al. (2015), *Deep Residual Learning* (ResNet), identified the **degradation problem**: a 56-layer plain CNN had *higher training error* than a 20-layer one — strictly an optimization failure. Residuals fixed it and won ImageNet; the idea then carried straight into transformers.

slides.title: The +1 that saves training
slides.body: Change each block from $y=F(x)$ to $y=x+F(x)$ (an identity *shortcut* around the transformation $F$). Differentiate: $\dfrac{\partial y}{\partial x}=I+\dfrac{\partial F}{\partial x}$. That additive **identity term $I$** is a gradient pathway of magnitude ~1 that *no depth can attenuate* — gradient reaches layer 1 of a 100-layer network essentially intact, regardless of what $F$'s Jacobian does. Same data, same LR: the residual network learns; the plain one doesn't. One `+x` removed the depth ceiling.

question.question: What is ∂/∂x of y = x + F(x)?
options: 1 + ∂F/∂x — the +1 from the identity path keeps gradients alive even if ∂F/∂x vanishes
question.explanation: Identity path derivative = 1; F path derivative = ∂F/∂x; sum = 1 + ∂F/∂x. That additive 1 is precisely what prevents vanishing gradients in deep stacks — even a layer that learns nothing still passes the gradient backward unchanged.

question.question: Write a residual layer's output y in terms of input x and the sublayer function F.
question.hint: Add the input to the sublayer's output.
question.explanation: y = x + F(x). The output is NOT just F(x) (that would be a plain layer) and NOT just x (that would skip the layer). It is the sum — F learns a *delta* to add to the running representation.

slides.title: Worked example: gradient through 50 layers
slides.body: Make it concrete. Suppose each block's local Jacobian has magnitude $0.9$. **Plain stack, 50 layers:** the gradient scales by $0.9^{50}\approx 0.005$ — early layers get ~0.5% of the signal: effectively untrained. **Residual stack:** each factor is $I+(\text{something})$, so the product stays $\mathcal{O}(1)$ rather than decaying to 0. Flip the local magnitude to $1.1$ and the *plain* stack explodes: $1.1^{50}\approx 117$. Residuals tame *both* failure modes by anchoring the per-layer multiplier near 1 — which is exactly what the $I$ in $I+\partial F/\partial x$ does.

question.question: Derive why residuals enable depth
question.goal: From: plain deep stacks won't train.

steps.prompt: Why do plain very-deep stacks fail to train?
steps.motivation: Each layer's Jacobian factor <1 multiplies across depth → gradients vanish.

options: Repeated <1 Jacobian factors make gradients vanish with depth

hints: Think product of many small numbers.
steps.reveal: Backprop multiplies per-layer factors; if each <1, deep products → 0.

steps.prompt: Write a residual block output and its derivative wrt x.
steps.motivation: The identity path contributes a +1 to the gradient so it can't vanish.
steps.reveal: y=x+F(x) ⇒ ∂y/∂x = I + F'(x): the I keeps gradient flowing at any depth.

slides.title: Part 3 — The residual stream (the modern mental model)
A shared bus every layer reads and writes
slides.body: Modern interpretability reframes the architecture around residuals: there is one $d_{model}$-wide **residual stream** running the full depth of the network. Each block *reads* it (through its LayerNorm'd input), computes a delta $F(\cdot)$, and *adds* that delta back. Information persists **by default** (the identity path) and is *edited incrementally* — not recomputed from scratch each layer. Attention writes/reads it, the FFN writes/reads it. This view explains why you can often ablate or reorder some blocks at inference with surprisingly small damage: each contributes a modest additive edit to a stream that already carries the answer.

slides.title: The 'skip connection' misconception
slides.body: It is *not* an occasional optional bypass. The residual path is the **main channel**; $F(x)$ is a *correction* added onto it. Calling it a 'skip' undersells it — most of the signal flows along the identity path, and the sublayers nudge it. Internalizing 'residual stream, not skip connection' is the difference between memorizing the formula and understanding why depth, ablation robustness, and the pre-norm placement (LayerNorm lesson) all work the way they do.

question.question: In the residual stream, what is a layer L attention sublayer's role?
options: Read from the stream (after LN), compute a per-token update, and add it back
Replace the stream entirely with attention's output
Stop gradient flow at this layer
question.explanation: It reads (LN-preprocessed), computes, and writes additively — augmenting the running representation, never replacing it. This additive-update view is the central abstraction of how transformer layers compose, and why the residual is not mere plumbing.

question.question: Diagnose the dead deep model.
question.scenario: A 48-layer plain (no-residual) transformer's training loss barely moves; an identical 48-layer model WITH residuals trains fine. Same data and learning rate.

rubricCriteria.description: no-residual: per-layer Jacobian factors (<1) multiply over 48 layers → gradient vanishes
with residual: d(x+F)/dx = I + F'(x) keeps an undiminished gradient path
so the residual model's depth-48 gradients survive and it learns

question.explanation: Depth alone isn't the problem — gradient propagation is. The residual identity term is what makes 48 layers trainable.

hints: Product of many numbers <1 over 48 layers → ?
slides.workedSolution: A plain deep stack multiplies ~48 sub-unity Jacobian factors → vanishing gradient. The residual adds an I term to the Jacobian — a gradient path of magnitude ~1 at any depth.

question.question: Why does adding residual connections rescue a very deep stack?
options: ∂y/∂x = I + F'(x): the identity term gives an undiminished gradient path through depth
question.explanation: Plain stacks multiply many <1 factors → 0. y=x+F(x) ⇒ ∂y/∂x = I + F'(x); the I is a gradient highway that doesn't vanish with depth.

question.prompt: Explain residual connections to your pet: the problem and the one-line fix.

rubricCriteria.description: deep plain nets vanish gradients (product of <1 factors)
the skip path is the identity, adding a +1 to the gradient
this lets very deep networks train

slides.title: Residuals beyond transformers
slides.body: This is not a transformer trick. ResNets (vision), U-Nets (diffusion models), residual blocks in graph and speech networks — anywhere people train deep, you see $x+F(x)$. The identity-path principle is one of the most transferable ideas in deep learning: whenever a deep stack won't train, the first question is "is there an un-normalized identity path for the gradient?"

slides.title: What to carry forward
slides.body: Residual $y=x+F(x)\Rightarrow\partial y/\partial x=I+\partial F/\partial x$: an undiminished gradient highway and a persistent information bus that *make depth work*. You now hold every component. Next: **assemble the transformer block** and see them compose into GPT-scale models.
